message.content: P2JW285000-0-A01600-1-.....XA A16 | Monday, October 12, 2026 THE WALL STREET JOURNAL OPINION # REVIEW & OUTLOOK # Trump's Diesel Insult to Lindsey Graham The world misses Lindsey Graham, and never more than now as President Trump sides more decidedly with Vladimir Putin in his war against Ukraine and Europe. The late Senator might have been able to persuade the President to avoid this moral and strategic mistake. Mr. Trump announced late Friday that the U.S. will buy up to 4.8 million tons (nearly 36 million barrels) of Russian diesel fuel in stages. That includes an "immediate" supply of 300,000 tons, another 500,000 in November, and one million "immediately thereafter." The delivery of another three million tons is "based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. The U.S. Treasury lifted some sanctions on Russia through April 7 so it could export the diesel. "Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. This is supposed to help Republicans in the November elections that are three weeks away. But 36 million barrels of Russian diesel won't make much. The world consumed 28 million barrels of diesel and other distillates daily in 2025, according to OPIS, which is part of Dow Jones Energy. What the deal will do is directly finance Mr. Putin's bloody war in Ukraine. And it may be worse. The Financial Times reported Saturday that the Trump Administration "threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing" to Kyiv if it continues attacking Russian refineries. In September Mr. Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel-fuel shortages with its long-range strikes on Russian refineries. Never mind Iranian and Houthi strikes on Middle Eastern energy production and transport. Russia helps Iran with intelligence and weapons. On Sunday Mr. Trump announced what he called "an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine supports such a cease-fire if Russia does the same, but as we write this Russia hasn't commented. An energy cease-fire would help both sides, as Ukraine faces another harsh winter and Russian refineries are under siege. But what about Mr. Putin's relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities? On Wednesday 22 people, including five children, were killed in a Russian cruise missile strike on an apartment building in the city of Pryluky. The next day a glide bomb hit two buses in Kramatorsk, killing 33. After the diesel announcement, Russia launched glide bombs Saturday at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20, including three children. Without a complete cease-fire, Russia will continue to torment Ukrainian civilians. The strategic turn here is hard to understand. Only last month Mr. Trump signed Lindsey Graham's bill to allow new sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. Now Mr. Trump has decided to buy Russian diesel and lift some current U.S. sanctions. The U.S. has been using Europe, India and China not to buy Russian oil, and so much for all that diplomatic effort. The Kremlin has been under financial pressure from Western sanctions and Ukraine's ability to hit targets in Russia. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates Russian oil companies will earn some $4.5 billion from the diesel deal. Mr. Trump added to the pressure on Ukraine by saying it's "time for Ukraine to get a new president." But he'll have to search far and wide for anyone in Ukraine who supports financing Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump complained again on the weekend that Mr. Zelensky could have settled the war many times. Yes, Kyiv could always surrender. Ukrainians prefer to fight for their independence and freedom. Eyeing a Nobel peace prize, Mr. Trump wants to broker a Russia-Ukraine peace, but the only pressure he ever applies is on Ukraine. His multiple attempts at appeasing Mr. Putin with sumptuity, flattery, offers of new investment, and more haven't moved the Russian. On the weekend a Russian official said the diesel deal doesn't change Mr. Putin's determination to achieve his war aim, which is to turn Ukraine into a Kremlin satyr. Until that changes, Mr. Trump's diesel deal helps Russia and not the cause of peace. # How to Make a Jihadist Martyr Jihadist killer Nidal Hasan deserves his future in hell, but before he gets there Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wants him to die before a firing squad open to the public for all to watch and record. This is a bad idea for many reasons, not least that it offers the killer the public martyrdom he craves. These columns don't oppose the death penalty. For some murders, it shows that a society is serious enough about its self-preservation to deliver retributive justice. Mr. Hasan killed 13 and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood in 2009 in the name of Islam. But his execution is best done quietly with few witnesses beyond officials and the families of the victims who wish to attend. This consigs him to history with ignominy but no fanfare. Mr. Hasan has said "I would still be a martyr" if executed, and that he killed those soldiers because they were "going against the Islamic Empire." A livestreamed death, complete with some incriminating last words, is what he wants. Mr. Hegseth seems to think a livestreamed execution by firing squad will be a show of U.S. resolve and deter others from such murderous acts. This misjudges the jihadist mind. It is a miscalculation that Western leaders often make about revolutionary jihadists like those who now run Iran. Mr. Hasan and his ilk understand they are likely to die. That is part of their fevered calculation. They imagine that by their violence they will contribute to the bloody caliphate they hope to build on earth. A public death by firing squad would give Mr. Hasan that publicity in perpetuity. It would assist the cult of death promoted by the perversion of Islam seeking to recruit more suicide attackers. Far from deterring jihadists, it would serve as a YouTube recruiting video. The U.S. doesn't need to execute Mr. Hasan on live TV to send a deterrent message. It needs to win the war against jihadists around the world, which at the moment means the fight against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Shiite revolution. If this weekend's attack on Riyadh is a guide, Mr. Hegseth has more urgent duties on that front. # Democrats vs. Alaska, Again The Alaska Senate race is a toss-up this year, which is remarkable given how Democrats in Washington keep demonstrating their zeal to stop economic development in the state. They did it again before they left town last month, blocking a bill that would have aided oil and gas development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR). In 2017 Congress required the Interior Secretary to create a plan for developing oil and gas in the ANWR coastal plain with a competitive program for leasing, developing and transporting the resources. The Biden Administration quickly suspended the leases in 2021 pending environmental review. Joe Biden's Interior Secretary later canceled the leases. The political seesaw left developers without enough confidence in stable policy to make the large investments required to get the region's rich reserves out of the ground. Trump II has opened more development leases for bidding, but companies are understandably wary of investing in projects that can be shut down by the next Democratic administration. In June the Bureau of Land Management's ANWR lease sale offered some 689,000 acres for lease but received bids on about 70,000 acres, worth about $3.7 million. Enter Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, who proposed to provide some federal assurance that the leases can't be canceled by the stroke of a pen. The Alaska's Right to Produce Act 2.0 would have prevented leases in the coastal plain oil and gas leasing program from being canceled unless the lessee is in violation of the lease terms. Democrats and the climate lobby blocked it from getting a vote on the Senate floor. Democrats of Wildlife said the bill would produce "rampant oil and gas drilling," while Sen. Martin Heinrich (D., N.M.) called it "another bill that would prioritize oil and gas over literally everything else." That's odd, since New Mexico is the major oil and gas producing state and Mr. Heinrich's constituents profit from it. The U.S. Energy Information Administration says New Mexico had 4.15 trillion cubic feet of gross natural gas withdrawals in 2025, far more than Alaska. Opponents say oil and gas leases in ANWR would destroy wildlife habitats, spoil the wilderness and infringe on sacred indigenous lands. But no one is proposing to pave the Arctic. If all of the 2026 leases offered had been purchased, the less than 700,000 acres would have been a small fraction of the more than 19 million acre wildlife refuge. Progressives want Alaska to be a nature preserve for tourism and dog-sled races. But the oil industry makes up a significant portion of Alaska's GDP, and future oil and gas leases will add jobs and tax revenue. It also serves America's energy needs and national-security interests. Across his two terms, Sen. Sullivan has been a champion for bringing investment to a state that needs more of both, while protecting the environment. His opponent, Mary Peltola, initially co-sporsored a version of this legislation when she was in the U.S. House. When the vote took place on the floor, she voted "present." Ms. Peltola could provide the 51st vote to give Democrats a majority, and then vote "present" to put even more of Alaska's vast energy resources in a deep political freeze. # LETTERS TO THE EDITOR # Massachusetts' Policies Increase Electric Bills Regarding your editorial "Climate Reality Hits Beacon Hill" (Oct. 8): The Northeast is dominated by blue-state governments where politicians are beholden to an unrealistic "green" agenda and are simultaneously desperate to talk about "affordability"—an incompatible combination. Opposition to domestic and reliable energy leads to the obstruction of pipeline projects. This in turn creates roadblocks toward getting natural gas from places like nearby Pennsylvania, the second-highest natural-gas-producing state. Natural gas is responsible for more than 40% of all electricity in the U.S., and the U.S. is the world's largest producer of natural gas. It should be a no-brainer. Yet in recent years, Massachusetts has implemented policies to become carbon neutral by 2050. That means less natural gas, oil and coal, and more solar and wind projects. Politicians have cheered the clo- sure of regional coal plants, perhaps most memorably in 2022 when former President Joe Biden stood before the state's last coal-fired power plant, Brayton Point Power Station, to discuss the climate "emergency." Forcibly removing reliable sources of energy from the grid doesn't make winter less harsh or homes warmer. It decreases supply, which leads to higher prices—Massachusetts' electricity prices are 40% to 60% higher than the national average—or forces an increased reliance on foreign supply. Politicians can be focused on climate or affordability, but they can't do both. Sadly, it's a lesson Massachusetts residents are about to learn when they open their electric bills this fall and winter. DANIEL TURNER Executive director and founder Power Point Round Hill, Va. # To Keep Medical Bills Low, Stay Out of the ER Regarding "Influencers Urge Public: Don't Pay Medical Bills" (Page One, Oct. 8): The U.S. has a growing medical bills: Don't go to the emergency room when you don't need to. ER bills are high partly because of the tremendous overhead required to provide 24/7 availability of life-saving medical care and expertise. As an ER physician, I see patients come to the ER for all sorts of complaints and then lament the high costs. Facility fees help cover the staffing and resources that allow ERs to respond to anything at a moment's notice. Yet the ER for an ankle sprain provides a patient medical care wherever and whenever he wants it. But that convenience comes with a cost. Waiting to see a primary-care physician or a walk-in clinic would result in a significantly lower bill. Using patient portals to get quick questions, seeking telehealth services, or consulting reputable online sources to determine whether something requires emergency services can save patients more than the 25% discount offered before a bill goes to collections. Simply not paying the bill exacerbates the problem by increasing hospital losses, potentially forcing them to raise charges to recoup those costs. Patients looking to reduce medical bills should skip the TikTok influencers and turn to traditional medical experts for guidance on where and when to seek care. LAURA DAYMUT, M.D. Omaha, Neb. # How to Help Lower Diesel Costs for Truckers Regarding "Diesel Prices Wearing Down Truckers" (U.S. News, Oct. 5): For decades, the biodiesel tax credit encouraged fuel retailers to blend biodiesel into petroleum diesel, expanding supply options while also driving demand for U.S. soybeans. Trucking customers reaped the benefits, realizing tangible savings with every gallon pumped into their tanks, and farmers had more demand for their soybeans. A rare win. But Congress allowed the biodiesel tax credit to lapse in 2024. This has ricocheted through the trucking sector, where fuel represents one of the industry's highest operating expenses. Losses of the biodiesel tax credit put upward pressure on the cost of all goods moved by truck. With more than 70% of all goods Americans purchase moving by truck, fuel prices are embedded in the cost of everything consumers buy. Reinstating the biodiesel tax credit is one of the clearest ways to help lower fuel costs and stabilize fuel supplies while strengthening demand for American agricultural products, benefiting families, farmers and our overall economy. If truck drivers are using every truck they can to address rising diesel fuel prices, then it's incumbent upon Congress to do the same. KARL McBRAYER President and CEO NATSO, representing truck stops and travel centers Alexandria, Va. # Rahm Emanuel Gets the Core American Principles Wrong In his op-ed "Washington Needs the Tax-Reform Spirit of '86" (Oct. 7), Rahm Emanuel writes at length about tax increases, mostly on business and capital, and even in duplicitate when he die; he saves conciseness for his discussion of spending cuts. While none of that is surprising for a potential political candidate, not so his final, shocking sentence: "Washington's goal should be to create wealth, not protect it." For 250 years our nation has grown on the exact opposite. We are a free people who work, innovate and invest to create wealth, and a government that protects it. Mr. Emanuel's formulation, a government that "produces" wealth, doesn't protect its citizens' property rights, has been a total failure everywhere it has been tried. It's less evocative of a revolutionary American "spirit of '86" than it is a Russian "duck of '17." MICHAEL MENDELSON Los Angeles # Justice Through Deterrence In their op-ed "Justice for Our Daughter Christa" (Oct. 7), Chris Bauer and Sharon Bauer make a lovely Christian case against the death penalty. But the purpose of the death penalty is to set a price tag on human life. The more lenient the punishment, the more likely homicide will appear to be an acceptable course of action. The death penalty for murder isn't barbaric. It is society's attempt to prevent future homicides. THOMAS F. BERNER Yonkers, N.Y. Letters intended for publication should be emailed to w.j.bauer@w.com.
